title: Switching One Part Off to Test It

scenes.tts: Watching a cell shows a part active alongside an outcome. It cannot show whether the part is needed. That takes removing the part. But a sodium current, a receptor or an enzyme cannot be pulled out of a living nerve by hand. A drug that binds one protein can switch that one part off within minutes, and often be washed out.
scenes.visual: A part sits in a chain with an outcome; the part is lifted out and a question mark replaces the outcome; a drug docks on the part, switches it off, and later floats away.
scenes.narration: Watching a cell shows a part active alongside an outcome. It cannot show whether the part is needed. That takes removing the part. But a sodium current, a receptor or an enzyme cannot be pulled out of a living nerve by hand. A drug that binds one protein can switch that one part off within minutes, and often be washed out.

scenes.tts: Choose a compound that binds one protein with high affinity. Tetrodotoxin binds voltage-gated sodium channels, one channel per toxin molecule, and plugs the pore, so no sodium passes. Curare binds the muscle acetylcholine receptor. Add tetrodotoxin to an axon and the action potential is blocked. The resting potential does not change.
scenes.visual: A compound docks on one protein; tetrodotoxin plugs a sodium channel and the idealised spike on the right goes flat while the resting level stays.
scenes.narration: Choose a compound that binds one protein with high affinity. scenes.tts: Deliver it where the target is. Use a bath on a slice, ionophoresis at a synapse, an injection into one eye, or a small muscimol injection into one brain area. Then show the drug works at that dose, by abolishing the response to a known agonist, or by recording the target's output.
scenes.visual: Four delivery routes drawn as small panels; then agonist alone gives a response and agonist after the drug gives none.
scenes.narration: Deliver it where the target is. Use a bath on a slice, ionophoresis at a synapse, an injection into one eye, or a small muscimol injection into one brain area. scenes.tts: Now measure the function you care about and the baseline side by side, with the drug on and off. Baseline is the control for general damage. A drug that blocks the induced change but leaves baseline alone shows the target is needed for induction under that protocol, not routine transmission.
scenes.visual: Idealised bars: induced change and baseline, drug off and on; the induced bar collapses, baseline stays.

scenes.tts: Here is an idealised example. Resting heart rate is seventy per minute. After atropine it is one hundred ten. After propranolol it is sixty-two. After both it is one hundred. So parasympathetic braking dominates at rest. This holds only if each drug fully blocks only its own division at that dose.
scenes.visual: Four bars (rest, atropine, propranolol, both) against a 70 line; a note and a caveat appear.

scenes.tts: Many drugs hit more than one target. The authors profiled sixty-five reportedly specific kinase inhibitors against seventy to eighty kinases. Many were not specific, so the authors urge considerable caution. So use the best-characterized drug at the lowest dose that works. Then add controls: a second drug from a different chemical series, and a matched inactive analogue. The best control is a drug-resistant target. One changed cysteine made fission yeast C R M one resistant to leptomycin B, and export stayed normal in the drug.
scenes.visual: One drug hits several targets; an idealised dose axis with the lowest working dose; two unrelated drugs and an inactive analogue; export blocked in normal CRM1 but continuing in the resistant one.

scenes.tts: In 1979 Pittman and Oppenheim immobilized chick embryos with curare and three toxins. With alpha-cobratoxin, about twenty-one thousand lumbar motoneurons survived to day ten, versus thirteen thousand five hundred in untreated controls. All four blockers were about equally effective, which argued against one drug's side effect. In 1986 Stryker and Harris injected tetrodotoxin, T T X, into both eyes of kittens. Ocular dominance columns, eye-specific stripes in cortex, did not form. Controls for the injection, systemic T T X and visual deprivation did not block them.
scenes.visual: Two findings in turn: motoneuron counts with four blockers, then kitten eyes injected and cortex stripes missing while the three controls keep their stripes.
scenes.caption: In 1979 Pittman and Oppenheim immobilized chick embryos with curare and three toxins. With alpha-cobratoxin, about 21,000 lumbar motoneurons survived to day 10, versus 13,500 in untreated controls. All four blockers were about equally effective, which argued against one drug's side effect. In 1986 Stryker and Harris injected tetrodotoxin (TTX) into both eyes of kittens. Ocular dominance columns, eye-specific stripes in cortex, did not form. Controls for the injection, systemic TTX and visual deprivation did not block them.

scenes.tts: In 1983 Collingridge, Kehl and McLennan applied A P V by ionophoresis, in doses that abolished responses to the N M D A agonist. In rat hippocampal slices, it had no effect on the field synaptic potential, but it prevented long-term potentiation. So the N M D A receptor is needed to start lasting change under that protocol, not for baseline transmission. Keep this rule. A block shows what is needed here, at this dose. It does not show what is enough.
scenes.visual: A schematic response plot: baseline unchanged under APV, no lasting rise after high-frequency stimulation; then the rule in a box.
